processing: Made as Wuyi rock tea is generally: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted. The category is defined by trade classification, not by a special method.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark twisted strips, less uniform than a single-cultivar lot may be.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges, sometimes of mixed size.
taste_profile: Varies by lot, since this is a category and not one cultivar. Expect the general Wuyi pattern of roast, mineral weight and some floral sweetness.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas. Lots vary, so taste a short first steep and adjust.

vintage_note: Sold, as other Wuyi rock teas are, by spring harvest year and roast. Older trade grades ran from special grade downwards, and today the word on a label may mean different things from seller to seller.
description:
Qi Zhong is less a single tea than a Wuyi trade category. Modern sellers use it for miscellaneous cultivars, set beside Da Hong Pao, Shui Xian, Rou Gui and the famous bushes.

The word also has a long history as a grade, so its meaning has shifted. The making is that of Wuyi rock tea generally: shaking, partial oxidation and roasting.

Because the leaf can vary, so does the cup. Expect roast and mineral weight with floral sweetness as the broad pattern of the class. Start with a short steep and adjust.

When buying, ask which cultivars went in and where they grew. In the mid-twentieth-century system, rock-grown and riverside qi zhong were separate grades, a distinction still worth asking about.
history:
In 1921 Jiang Shunan sorted rock teas into four ranks, among them upper qi zhong and qi zhong. Later classifiers Liao Cunren and Lin Fuquan kept the term, with Lin dividing it further into famous-bush, single-bush and top qi zhong.

In the 1950s and 1960s, rock qi zhong and riverside qi zhong were listed as separate classes. After 1949 commercial qi zhong was graded from special grade to fourth grade, and from the 1970s Shui Xian and qi zhong shared a scale of eleven grades.
